claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Himes and Zhang, 2018; Xue et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The assignment of states is unreliable for similar structures that can only be distinguished using high-resolution detail.
claims.source: However, the assignment of states is unreliable for similar structures that can only be distinguished using high-resolution detail, and statistical approaches to quantitatively assess classification results are lacking.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference about the limitations of current methods.

claims.claim: Statistical approaches to quantitatively assess classification results are lacking.
claims.source: However, the assignment of states is unreliable for similar structures that can only be distinguished using high-resolution detail, and statistical approaches to quantitatively assess classification results are lacking.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of the field.

claims.claim: Machine learning has been employed for particle classification in tomograms, but currently only performs as well as a human operator.
claims.source: Machine learning has been employed for particle classification in tomograms, but currently only performs as well as a human operator (Moebel et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Moebel et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Machine learning algorithms perform better than 3D template matching at molecule localization in tomograms, but classification remains challenging for all algorithms.
claims.source: While machine learning algorithms perform better than 3D template matching at molecule localization in tomograms, classification remains challenging for all algorithms (Gubins et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gubins et al., 2020).

claims.claim: 2DTM uses molecular models from in vitro structure determination or in silico structure prediction to generate a 3D density.
claims.source: 2DTM uses molecular models, from in vitro structure determination or in silico structure prediction (e.g. Alphafold2 Jumper et al., 2021) to generate a 3D density.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the methodology of 2DTM and cites Alphafold2 as an example (Jumper et al., 2021).

claims.claim: 2DTM calculates millions of 2D projections representing different orientations of the molecule.
claims.source: This 3D density (hereafter referred to as the template) is then used to calculate millions of 2D projections representing different orientations of the molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the 2DTM methodology.

claims.claim: A pixel-wise cross-correlation of the 2D projections with a high-resolution 2D cryo-EM image is performed, yielding a 2DTM signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the best matching projection at every pixel location.
claims.source: A pixel-wise cross-correlation of the 2D projections with a high-resolution 2D cryo-EM image is performed, yielding a 2DTM signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the best matching projection at every pixel location (Rickgauer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the 2DTM methodology and is supported by a citation (Rickgauer et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The 2DTM SNR values are subjected to a significance test by comparison to a Gaussian noise distribution following a matched filter.
claims.source: The 2DTM SNR values are subjected to a significance test by comparison to a Gaussian noise distribution following a matched filter, which is used to establish a threshold allowing a given number of false positives (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the 2DTM methodology and is supported by citations (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The 2DTM SNR is proportional to template mass.
claims.source: The 2DTM SNR is proportional to template mass and negatively affected by non-matching elements between template and target (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2020; Rickgauer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2020; Rickgauer et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The 2DTM SNR is negatively affected by non-matching elements between template and target.
claims.source: The 2DTM SNR is proportional to template mass and negatively affected by non-matching elements between template and target (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2020; Rickgauer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2020; Rickgauer et al., 2017).

claims.claim: A template generated from a Bacillus subtilis 50S large ribosomal subunit was able to detect 50S in 2D cryo-EM images of Mycoplasma pneumoniae cells, but with a lower average 2DTM SNR compared to a M. pneumoniae 50S template.
claims.source: We have shown that a template generated from a Bacillus subtilis 50S large ribosomal subunit was able to detect 50S in 2D cryo-EM images of Mycoplasma pneumoniae cells, but with a lower average 2DTM SNR compared to a M. pneumoniae 50S template (Lucas et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Lucas et al., 2021).

claims.claim: 2DTM using partially matching templates can be sufficiently sensitive to yield significant targets.
claims.source: This demonstrated that (1) 2DTM using partially matching templates can be sufficiently sensitive to yield significant targets and (2) the mean 2DTM SNR of detected targets provides a read-out of the relative similarity between different templates and populations of particle species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior experimental results.

claims.claim: The mean 2DTM SNR of detected targets provides a read-out of the relative similarity between different templates and populations of particle species.
claims.source: This demonstrated that (1) 2DTM using partially matching templates can be sufficiently sensitive to yield significant targets and (2) the mean 2DTM SNR of detected targets provides a read-out of the relative similarity between different templates and populations of particle species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior experimental results.

claims.claim: 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis intermediates are of a similar size and share significant structure with one another, making them difficult to separate at low resolution.
claims.source: As a model system, we chose to examine the late stages of 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae because (1) intermediates are of a similar size and share significant structure with one another, making them difficult to separate at low resolution, (2) molecular models spanning multiple late intermediate states have recently been described, and (3) the maturation events that occur before and after nuclear export have been characterized.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about 60S ribosome biogenesis.

claims.claim: Molecular models spanning multiple late intermediate states of 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis have recently been described.
claims.source: As a model system, we chose to examine the late stages of 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae because (1) intermediates are of a similar size and share significant structure with one another, making them difficult to separate at low resolution, (2) molecular models spanning multiple late intermediate states have recently been described, and (3) the maturation events that occur before and after nuclear export have been characterized.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about available structural models.

claims.claim: The maturation events of 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis that occur before and after nuclear export have been characterized.
claims.source: As a model system, we chose to examine the late stages of 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae because (1) intermediates are of a similar size and share significant structure with one another, making them difficult to separate at low resolution, (2) molecular models spanning multiple late intermediate states have recently been described, and (3) the maturation events that occur before and after nuclear export have been characterized.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about 60S ribosome biogenesis.

claims.claim: Subcellular localization can validate the assignment of intermediate and mature states of 60S ribosomal subunits.
claims.source: Subcellular localization can thereby validate the assignment of intermediate and mature states.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known biology of 60S maturation.

claims.claim: 2DTM can locate and distinguish nuclear intermediates of 60S maturation in 2D cryo-EM images of focused ion beam (FIB)-milled yeast cells.
claims.source: We show that 2DTM can locate and distinguish nuclear intermediates of 60S maturation in 2D cryo-EM images of focused ion beam (FIB)-milled yeast cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: 2DTM can distinguish predefined 60S populations separated by subcellular localization.
claims.source: We confirm that 2DTM can distinguish predefined 60S populations separated by subcellular localization and identify compositional differences between them.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: 2DTM can identify compositional differences between 60S populations.
claims.source: We confirm that 2DTM can distinguish predefined 60S populations separated by subcellular localization and identify compositional differences between them.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: A maximum likelihood-based approach can identify two sub-populations of nuclear intermediates that were not otherwise separable.
claims.source: We apply a maximum likelihood-based approach to identify two sub-populations of nuclear intermediates that were not otherwise separable and provide a confidence of single particle classification.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: A maximum likelihood-based approach can provide a confidence of single particle classification.
claims.source: We apply a maximum likelihood-based approach to identify two sub-populations of nuclear intermediates that were not otherwise separable and provide a confidence of single particle classification.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the methodology described in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The nuclear pre-60S intermediate population shifts to a more mature intermediate after inhibiting Crm1-mediated nuclear export.
claims.source: We show that using this approach, we can observe a shift in the nuclear pre-60S intermediate population to a more mature intermediate after inhibiting Crm1-mediated nuclear export.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Different particle populations in cells can be modelled with a Gaussian distribution of their relative 2DTM SNR ratios to effectively distinguish related complexes.
claims.source: This study demonstrates that different particle populations in cells can be modelled with a Gaussian distribution of their relative 2DTM SNR ratios to effectively distinguish related complexes and identify population changes in cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the methodology and results presented in Figures 3 and 6.

claims.claim: Gaussian distribution of relative 2DTM SNR ratios can identify population changes in cells.
claims.source: This study demonstrates that different particle populations in cells can be modelled with a Gaussian distribution of their relative 2DTM SNR ratios to effectively distinguish related complexes and identify population changes in cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing changes after Crm1 inhibition.

claims.claim: 2DTM identified 4363 large ribosomal subunits in 28 2D cryo-EM images of the nuclear periphery of 7 lamellae generated from actively growing Sacchromyces cerevisiae cells.
claims.source: We identified 4363 large ribosomal subunits by 2DTM using a template generated from a model representing the mature 60S (PDB: 6Q8Y) (Tesina et al., 2019; Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The peaks corresponding to significant detections were clearly distinguishable from background.
claims.source: The peaks corresponding to significant detections were clearly distinguishable from background (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), enabling precise localization of mature 60S in the cell.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: 2DTM enables precise localization of mature 60S in the cell.
claims.source: The peaks corresponding to significant detections were clearly distinguishable from background (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), enabling precise localization of mature 60S in the cell.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: No significant mature 60S-detected targets were observed in regions of the image corresponding to the vacuole.
claims.source: Consistent with the expected high specificity of 2DTM, we did not observe any significant mature 60S-detected targets in regions of the image corresponding to the vacuole (Figure 1C and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and G.

claims.claim: 229 mature 60S-detected targets localized to the nucleus, representing ~5% of all mature 60S identified targets.
claims.source: In contrast, 229 mature 60S-detected targets localized to the nucleus, representing ~5% of all mature 60S identified targets in these images, well above the expected one false positive per image (Figure 1C–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The number of nuclear mature 60S-detected targets is well above the expected one false positive per image.
claims.source: In contrast, 229 mature 60S-detected targets localized to the nucleus, representing ~5% of all mature 60S identified targets in these images, well above the expected one false positive per image (Figure 1C–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of observed detections with expected false positive rate.

claims.claim: The normalized maximum intensity projections (MIPs) have a distribution of values similar in shape and location of their maxima in different regions of the image, corresponding to the nucleus, cytoplasm, and vacuole.
claims.source: We found that the normalized maximum intensity projections (MIPs) have a distribution of values similar in shape and location of their maxima in different regions of the image, corresponding to the nucleus, cytoplasm, and vacuole.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The probability of false positives is similar in different compartments (nucleus, cytoplasm, vacuole).
claims.source: This indicates that the probability of a false positives is also similar in these different compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of MIP distributions.

claims.claim: The slight differences in the MIP distributions between the compartments likely result from differences in their composition.
claims.source: The slight differences in the MIP distributions between the compartments likely result from differences in their composition.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of observed differences.

claims.claim: False detections are not more likely in visibly darker or denser regions of the image.
claims.source: We conclude that false detections are not more likely in visibly darker or denser regions of the image.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the MIP distribution analysis.

claims.claim: The median density of 60S in the cytoplasm is ~6500 60S/μm3.
claims.source: In regions of the images corresponding to the cytoplasm we observe a median density of ~6500 60S/μm3, which, assuming an average cell volume of ~42 μm3 of which ~65% is cytoplasm, corresponds to a total of ~180,000 60S/cell (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The observed cytoplasmic 60S density corresponds to a total of ~180,000 60S/cell.
claims.source: In regions of the images corresponding to the cytoplasm we observe a median density of ~6500 60S/μm3, which, assuming an average cell volume of ~42 μm3 of which ~65% is cytoplasm, corresponds to a total of ~180,000 60S/cell (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on calculation from observed density and assumed cell volume.

claims.claim: The estimated total of ~180,000 60S/cell is consistent with prior estimates of 187,000 ± 56,000 ribosomes per yeast cell based on rRNA concentration.
claims.source: This is consistent with prior estimates of 187,000 ± 56,000 ribosomes per yeast cell based on rRNA concentration (von der Haar, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim compares the current results with prior published estimates (von der Haar, 2008).

claims.claim: The median density of 60S in the nucleus was ~30-fold lower than in the cytoplasm at ~200 60S/µm3.
claims.source: The median density in the nucleus was ~30-fold lower at ~200 60S/µm3 (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The lower density of 60S particles in the nucleus agrees with previously observed lower density of 60S particles in the nucleus.
claims.source: This agrees with the previously observed lower density of 60S particles in the nucleus, e.g. (Delavoie et al., 2019), but likely only reflects a subset of the nuclear 60S population.
claims.evidence: The claim compares current results with prior observations (Delavoie et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The observed nuclear 60S density likely only reflects a subset of the nuclear 60S population.
claims.source: This agrees with the previously observed lower density of 60S particles in the nucleus, e.g. (Delavoie et al., 2019), but likely only reflects a subset of the nuclear 60S population.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the completeness of detection.

claims.claim: Mature 60S-detected targets were oriented with their polypeptide exit tunnels facing the cytoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope.
claims.source: We found that mature 60S-detected targets were oriented with their polypeptide exit tunnels facing the cytoplasmic surface of the NE but were depleted from within ~20 nm of the vacuole (Figure 1C and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claims.claim: Mature 60S-detected targets were depleted from within ~20 nm of the vacuole.
claims.source: We found that mature 60S-detected targets were oriented with their polypeptide exit tunnels facing the cytoplasmic surface of the NE but were depleted from within ~20 nm of the vacuole (Figure 1C and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claims.claim: The orientation of 60S identified by 2DTM is unlikely to be an artefact introduced by features of the membrane in the image.
claims.source: This indicates that the orientation of 60S identified by 2DTM is unlikely to be an artefact introduced by features of the membrane in the image.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the biologically relevant orientations observed.

claims.claim: A 3D reconstruction generated using the locations and orientations of 3991 significant mature 60S-detected targets shows density reminiscent of the 40S small ribosomal subunit in addition to the 60S.
claims.source: To confirm that the targets identified with the mature 60S template reflect ribosomes, we generated a 3D reconstruction using the locations and orientations of 3991 significant mature 60S-detected targets using standard single particle approaches as described previously (Lucas et al., 2021). In addition to the 60S, the 10 Å-filtered reconstruction shows density reminiscent of the 40S small ribosomal subunit (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: The presence of 40S density in the reconstruction is consistent with many of the mature 60S detected targets representing a population of 80S ribosomes.
claims.source: This is consistent with many of the mature 60S detected targets representing a population of 80S ribosomes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed 40S density.

claims.claim: The resolution of the 40S is lower relative to the 60S in the reconstruction.
claims.source: Local resolution estimation shows that the resolution of the 40S is lower relative to the 60S (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The lower resolution of the 40S follows the expected positional heterogeneity of the 40S relative to the 60S when capturing ribosomes in a range of translation states.
claims.source: This follows the expected positional heterogeneity of the 40S relative to the 60S when capturing ribosomes in a range of translation states (Freitas et al., 2021; Korostelev, 2022) and prior results using 50S Mycoplasma pneumoniae targets (Lucas et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citations to prior work (Freitas et al., 2021; Korostelev, 2022; Lucas et al., 2021).

claims.claim: 2DTM-identified locations and orientations in 2D cryo-EM images of FIB-milled lamellae reflect biologically relevant locations and orientations of ribosomes in the cell.
claims.source: We conclude that 2DTM-identified locations and orientations in 2D cryo-EM images of FIB-milled lamellae reflect biologically relevant locations and orientations of ribosomes in the cell.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The nuclear envelope (NE) creates a physical barrier that separates premature 60S in the nucleus from mature 60S in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: The nuclear envelope (NE) creates a physical barrier that separates premature 60S in the nucleus from mature 60S in the cytoplasm and is easily distinguishable in many 2D images by its characteristic double membrane and by the more granular appearance of the cytoplasm vs the nucleus (e.g. Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claims.claim: The nuclear envelope is easily distinguishable in many 2D images by its characteristic double membrane and by the more granular appearance of the cytoplasm vs the nucleus.
claims.source: The nuclear envelope (NE) creates a physical barrier that separates premature 60S in the nucleus from mature 60S in the cytoplasm and is easily distinguishable in many 2D images by its characteristic double membrane and by the more granular appearance of the cytoplasm vs the nucleus (e.g. Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The nuclear 60S detected with the mature 60S template may result from cross-detection of nuclear precursors, which share part of their structure with mature 60S.
claims.source: Our observation of a substantial population of mature 60S-detected targets in the nucleus, but not in the vacuole (Figure 1C and G), suggests that the nuclear 60S may result from cross-detection of nuclear precursors, which share part of their structure with mature 60S and therefore also produce significant correlations (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on observed data.

claims.claim: The LN 60S represents the most mature nuclear intermediate for which there is a structure.
claims.source: The LN 60S was chosen because it represents the most mature nuclear intermediate for which there is a structure, and which retains ribosome biogenesis factors (RBFs) that are removed during nuclear and early cytoplasmic processing (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about available structures.

claims.claim: The LN 60S retains ribosome biogenesis factors (RBFs) that are removed during nuclear and early cytoplasmic processing.
claims.source: The LN 60S was chosen because it represents the most mature nuclear intermediate for which there is a structure, and which retains ribosome biogenesis factors (RBFs) that are removed during nuclear and early cytoplasmic processing (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about 60S maturation.

claims.claim: The similarities between the mature 60S and LN 60S structures will result in cross-detection of the respective other complex.
claims.source: Thus, we expect that (1) the similarities between the mature 60S and LN 60S structures will result in cross-detection of the respective other complex and (2) the cytoplasmic population will more closely resemble the mature 60S and nuclear population will more closely resemble the LN 60S resulting in a higher mature 60S / LN 60S 2DTM SNR ratio in the cytoplasm than the nucleus.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the structural similarity of the templates.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic population will more closely resemble the mature 60S and nuclear population will more closely resemble the LN 60S resulting in a higher mature 60S / LN 60S 2DTM SNR ratio in the cytoplasm than the nucleus.
claims.source: Thus, we expect that (1) the similarities between the mature 60S and LN 60S structures will result in cross-detection of the respective other complex and (2) the cytoplasmic population will more closely resemble the mature 60S and nuclear population will more closely resemble the LN 60S resulting in a higher mature 60S / LN 60S 2DTM SNR ratio in the cytoplasm than the nucleus.
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the known biology of 60S maturation.

claims.claim: 1651 significant LN 60S-detected targets were located in 28 images of the nucleus and nuclear periphery.
claims.source: In the 28 images of the nucleus and nuclear periphery we located 1651 significant LN 60S-detected targets of which 1382 (~84%) of the LN 60S-detected targets were cytoplasmic and 268 (16%) were nuclear, a three-fold greater proportion than the mature 60S-detected targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: 1382 (~84%) of the LN 60S-detected targets were cytoplasmic and 268 (16%) were nuclear.
claims.source: In the 28 images of the nucleus and nuclear periphery we located 1651 significant LN 60S-detected targets of which 1382 (~84%) of the LN 60S-detected targets were cytoplasmic and 268 (16%) were nuclear, a three-fold greater proportion than the mature 60S-detected targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The proportion of nuclear LN 60S-detected targets is three-fold greater than the mature 60S-detected targets.
claims.source: In the 28 images of the nucleus and nuclear periphery we located 1651 significant LN 60S-detected targets of which 1382 (~84%) of the LN 60S-detected targets were cytoplasmic and 268 (16%) were nuclear, a three-fold greater proportion than the mature 60S-detected targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data.

claims.claim: More cytoplasmic than nuclear targets were identified in 2DTM searches with both mature and LN 60S templates because the cytoplasm represented a larger area of the images.
claims.source: We identified more cytoplasmic than nuclear targets in 2DTM searches with both mature and LN 60S templates because (1) the cytoplasm represented a larger area of our images and (2) the concentration of 60S is expected to be higher in the cytoplasm relative to the nucleus.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design.

claims.claim: More cytoplasmic than nuclear targets were identified in 2DTM searches with both mature and LN 60S templates because the concentration of 60S is expected to be higher in the cytoplasm relative to the nucleus.
claims.source: We identified more cytoplasmic than nuclear targets in 2DTM searches with both mature and LN 60S templates because (1) the cytoplasm represented a larger area of our images and (2) the concentration of 60S is expected to be higher in the cytoplasm relative to the nucleus.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claims.claim: Only one of the significant LN 60S-detected targets localized to the vacuole, which is below the expected false positive rate.
claims.source: Only one of the significant LN 60S-detected targets localized to the vacuole, which is below the expected false positive rate and further indicates the specificity of 2DTM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with expected false positive rate.

claims.claim: The low number of LN 60S-detected targets in the vacuole further indicates the specificity of 2DTM.
claims.source: Only one of the significant LN 60S-detected targets localized to the vacuole, which is below the expected false positive rate and further indicates the specificity of 2DTM.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the low false positive rate.

claims.claim: The locations of many of the targets identified in the mature and LN 60S searches overlap.
claims.source: As expected from the similarity between the mature and LN 60S templates, the locations of many of the targets identified in the two searches overlap (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: Approximately one third of the mature 60S-detected targets overlapped with LN 60S-detected targets.
claims.source: Approximately one third of the mature 60S-detected targets overlapped with LN 60S-detected targets while 92% of the LN 60S-detected targets overlapped with mature 60S-detected targets (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: 92% of the LN 60S-detected targets overlapped with mature 60S-detected targets.
claims.source: Approximately one third of the mature 60S-detected targets overlapped with LN 60S-detected targets while 92% of the LN 60S-detected targets overlapped with mature 60S-detected targets (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: 30% of the nuclear targets were LN 60S-detected only, compared to only 0.5% of the cytoplasmic targets.
claims.source: Combining the results of both searches, 30% of the nuclear targets were LN 60S-detected only, compared to only 0.5% of the cytoplasmic targets (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The median log2(mature 60S / LN 60S 2DTM SNR) values of targets identified with both templates were significantly higher for the cytoplasmic population than the nuclear population (P<0.0001, K-S. test).
claims.source: Consistent with their expected localizations, the median log2(mature 60S / LN 60S 2DTM SNR) values of targets identified with both templates were significantly higher for the cytoplasmic population than the nuclear population (P<0.0001, K-S. test) (Figure 2D–G and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D-G and J.

claims.claim: 94% of the 1361 cytoplasmic targets detected with both templates have a closer match (higher SNR) with the mature 60S.
claims.source: Of the population detected with both mature and LN 60S templates, 94% of the 1361 cytoplasmic targets have a closer match (higher SNR) with the mature 60S and 88% of the 171 nuclear targets have a closer match with the LN 60S (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: 88% of the 171 nuclear targets detected with both templates have a closer match with the LN 60S.
claims.source: Of the population detected with both mature and LN 60S templates, 94% of the 1361 cytoplasmic targets have a closer match (higher SNR) with the mature 60S and 88% of the 171 nuclear targets have a closer match with the LN 60S (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: 98% of the cytoplasmic targets are annotated as mature 60S when combining all 60S-detected targets.
claims.source: Combining all 60S-detected targets, the nuclear 60S targets are now more clearly distinguished from the cytoplasmic population with 98% of the cytoplasmic targets annotated as mature 60S, and 60% of the nuclear targets annotated as pre-60S (Figure 2K and L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claims.claim: 60% of the nuclear targets are annotated as pre-60S when combining all 60S-detected targets.
claims.source: Combining all 60S-detected targets, the nuclear 60S targets are now more clearly distinguished from the cytoplasmic population with 98% of the cytoplasmic targets annotated as mature 60S, and 60% of the nuclear targets annotated as pre-60S (Figure 2K and L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claims.claim: The ~40% of nuclear targets that more closely resemble the mature 60S likely reflect nuclear intermediates different from the LN 60S.
claims.source: The ~40% of nuclear targets that more closely resemble the mature 60S likely reflect nuclear intermediates different from the LN 60S (see below) and thus do not perfectly match either template.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the identity of these targets.

claims.claim: Comparing 2DTM SNRs can effectively differentiate populations of related particles in situ.
claims.source: We conclude that comparing 2DTM SNRs can effectively differentiate populations of related particles in situ.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The nuclear and cytoplasmic 60S populations were significantly different with respect to their relative similarity to the LN and mature 60S.
claims.source: We show above that the nuclear and cytoplasmic 60S populations were significantly different with respect to their relative similarity to the LN and mature 60S (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Classifying targets by their highest 2DTM SNR effectively separates the nuclear from the cytoplasmic population.
claims.source: We also show that classifying targets by their highest 2DTM SNR effectively separates the nuclear from the cytoplasmic population (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A single threshold does not fully capture the differences between the nuclear and cytoplasmic populations.
claims.source: However, a single threshold does not fully capture the differences between the nuclear and cytoplasmic populations and for an individual particle the confidence of classification is unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the limitations of threshold-based classification.

claims.claim: For an individual particle the confidence of classification using a single threshold is unclear.
claims.source: However, a single threshold does not fully capture the differences between the nuclear and cytoplasmic populations and for an individual particle the confidence of classification is unclear.

results.result: 2DTM successfully localizes 60S ribosomal subunits in FIB-milled yeast cells with high precision and specificity, identifying 4363 targets in 28 images with biologically relevant locations and orientations.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 provide quantitative detection data showing 4363 60S targets with clear peaks distinguishable from background, minimal false positives in vacuoles, and appropriate subcellular distribution. Claims C64, C173-C174 confirm biological relevance through orientation analysis and 3D reconstruction (C60-C63), validating that FIB-milling preserves high-resolution signal for 2DTM detection.

results.result: Comparing 2DTM SNR ratios using mature and LN 60S templates effectively differentiates nuclear pre-60S from cytoplasmic mature 60S populations based on subcellular localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 provide statistical evidence (p<0.0001) showing significantly higher mature/LN SNR ratios in cytoplasm vs nucleus, with 94% of cytoplasmic targets matching mature 60S and 88% of nuclear targets matching LN 60S. The overlap analysis (C80-C82) and classification results (C86-C87) demonstrate effective separation validated by known biology (C65-C66).

results.result: A maximum likelihood approach using Gaussian mixture models provides quantitative confidence metrics for single-particle classification, effectively separating nuclear and cytoplasmic 60S populations with specified probabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 demonstrate excellent model fit (R²=0.993) with means matching independently calculated nuclear (-0.026) and cytoplasmic (0.335) populations. Claims C102-C104 show the method assigns appropriate confidence thresholds (95% and 50%) consistent with biological expectations. The approach provides particle-level probability assignments (C105, C190-C191) addressing a key limitation identified in C92-C93.

results.result: 2DTM with three templates (EN, LN, mature 60S) classifies at least three distinct 60S maturation states from <500 molecules, with EN 60S predominantly nuclear (70%), LN 60S evenly distributed, and mature 60S predominantly cytoplasmic (85%).
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C167 provide quantitative classification data showing biologically consistent subcellular distributions for three maturation states. The EN 60S population (C157-C159) shows 43% nuclear localization with >3-fold fewer cytoplasmic targets than LN 60S, consistent with earlier maturation stage. Claims C162-C164 demonstrate detection of population heterogeneity, and C182-C184 confirm classification from small populations.

results.result: Inhibiting Crm1-mediated nuclear export with Leptomycin B causes accumulation of late nuclear intermediates, with >90% of nuclear targets shifting to LN 60S classification and loss of Nog2 occupancy differences between compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C142, C168-C169 show increased nuclear pre-60S density and shift to >90% LN 60S classification after export inhibition. Claims C143-C147 demonstrate that Nog1 (removed post-export) still differentiates compartments while Nog2 (removed pre-export) no longer does, consistent with accumulation of export-competent Nog2-lacking intermediates. This provides biological validation of the classification method (C170, C238).

results.result: Modified 2DTM templates reveal that ribosome biogenesis factors, particularly Nog1 and Nog2, differentiate nuclear from cytoplasmic 60S populations, with rRNA contributing 1.5-1.8 fold more to SNR than proteins despite only 1.25-fold greater mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C136 provide quantitative analysis showing LN 60S proteins contribute positively to nuclear target SNR and negatively to cytoplasmic targets. Claims C137-C141 demonstrate that Nog1 and Nog2 (50% of RBF mass) differentiate compartments in cells with active export, consistent with known biology (C138-C140). The template truncation experiments (C133-C134) validate compositional differences.

results.result: The mean log2 SNR ratio is largely independent of absolute SNR values and can be predicted from template structures alone, with simulated mature 60S showing mean 0.337 matching observed cytoplasmic population (p=0.867).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 show only ~10% difference in mean log2 ratios between top and bottom 20% of targets by SNR. Claims C119-C121 demonstrate simulation agreement with experimental data for cytoplasmic population. This independence from image SNR (C199-C200) enables model validation and suggests cytoplasmic population closely matches mature 60S template.

results.result: The nuclear 60S population deviates from predicted SNR ratios and fits a single Gaussian poorly, indicating a more complex mixture of maturation states distinct from both mature and LN 60S templates.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 show nuclear population deviates from simulation predictions, unlike cytoplasmic population. Claims C150-C151 demonstrate poor single Gaussian fit with mean log2 near 0, suggesting additional populations. Claims C236-C237 confirm presence of at least one additional pre-60S population (Figure 6), supporting the complexity inference (C126).

results.result: An EN 60S population with 5S rRNP rotated 180° was identified accounting for >50% of nuclear 60S, and a nuclear LN 60S population was detected, suggesting temporal lag between 5S rotation/ITS2 removal and nuclear export.
results.evaluation: Claim C243 identifies EN 60S population consistent with in vitro structures (Leidig et al., 2014). Claim C245 shows this population represents >50% of nuclear 60S, arguing for on-pathway intermediate despite prior difficulty establishing in vivo presence (C244). Claims C246-C247 identify nuclear LN 60S population implying temporal lag, though C248 acknowledges need for flux studies to test this hypothesis more thoroughly.

results.result: 2DTM detects ~6500 60S/μm³ in cytoplasm corresponding to ~180,000 60S/cell, consistent with prior rRNA-based estimates, and ~200 60S/μm³ in nucleus (~30-fold lower).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 provide density measurements with calculation based on assumed cell volume (42 μm³, 65% cytoplasm). Claim C53 shows agreement with prior estimate of 187,000±56,000 ribosomes/cell (von der Haar, 2008). Claims C54-C55 show lower nuclear density consistent with prior observations, though C56 acknowledges this likely reflects subset of nuclear population.

results.result: Mature 60S-detected targets are oriented with polypeptide exit tunnels facing the cytoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope and depleted within ~20 nm of vacuole, indicating biologically relevant orientations.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 describe specific orientations at nuclear envelope and depletion near vacuole. Claim C59 infers these orientations are unlikely artifacts based on biological relevance. The orientation analysis provides validation that 2DTM identifies genuine ribosomes in functionally appropriate locations.

results.result: 3D reconstruction from 3991 mature 60S-detected targets shows density for 40S subunit in addition to 60S, with lower 40S resolution consistent with positional heterogeneity in translation states.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 shows 40S density in reconstruction, supporting that targets represent 80S ribosomes (C61). Claims C62-C63 explain lower 40S resolution as expected from positional heterogeneity during translation, consistent with prior work (Freitas et al., 2021; Korostelev, 2022; Lucas et al., 2021). This validates that detected targets are genuine ribosomes.

results.result: Normalized maximum intensity projections show similar distributions across nucleus, cytoplasm, and vacuole, indicating similar false positive probability across compartments and that false detections are not more likely in darker/denser regions.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 shows similar MIP distributions across compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Claim C48 infers similar false positive probability from distribution similarity. Claim C50 concludes false detections not biased by image density. However, C49 is speculative about causes of slight differences. This analysis validates that compartment-based classification is not confounded by differential false positive rates.

results.result: Overfitting contributes substantially to variance in individual 2DTM SNRs (estimated ~40% bias at threshold), but effect is reduced for SNR ratios when using similar templates, with Gaussian modeling accounting for this bias in classification.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 establish theoretical basis for overfitting with 243 degrees of freedom yielding apparent noise SNR of 3.31. Claims C111-C112 show proportionally greater effect at low SNR but substantial reduction when comparing similar templates. Claims C203-C210 explain how Gaussian modeling captures these factors, accounting for bias in probability calculations. This provides important methodological context for classification reliability.

results.result: Cytoplasmic targets detected by both EN and LN 60S show single population resembling LN 60S, while nuclear targets show at least two distinct populations based on relative similarity to EN, LN, and mature 60S templates.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C164 describe distributions of SNR ratios for targets detected by multiple templates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D). The cytoplasmic homogeneity vs nuclear heterogeneity supports the maturation pathway model and validates the classification approach. This demonstrates the method can detect population complexity beyond simple binary classification.

results.result: LN 60S template detected 1651 targets (84% cytoplasmic, 16% nuclear), with three-fold greater nuclear proportion than mature 60S and only one vacuole target (below false positive rate).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 provide detection statistics showing expected enrichment of LN 60S in nucleus relative to mature 60S. Claims C75-C76 explain higher cytoplasmic counts by larger imaging area and higher concentration. Claims C77-C78 show low vacuole detection confirming specificity. This demonstrates the LN 60S template successfully enriches for nuclear intermediates.

results.result: 2DTM enables single-molecule classification from fewer images than traditional reference-free methods, potentially distinguishing populations from single images given sufficient target abundance.
results.evaluation: Claim C185 suggests single-image classification is possible with sufficient abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). Claims C186-C187 contrast with traditional methods requiring hundreds-thousands of particles. However, the single-image capability is presented as inference rather than demonstrated systematically. The advantage over traditional methods is conceptually sound but not rigorously validated.

results.result: Classification requires aligned molecular models producing correlation peaks at same pixel location; imperfect rotational matches or differences in model quality may affect SNR ratios and classification.
results.evaluation: Claim C211 states methodological requirement for template alignment. Claims C212-C213 identify potential sources of error from rotational matching and model quality differences. These are reasonable concerns based on the methodology, though their actual impact is not quantified experimentally. This represents important methodological limitations.

results.result: Templates were generated from maps at 3.1-3.5 Å resolution, with mature 60S potentially more accurate due to more available structures; this may partially explain better agreement of cytoplasmic vs nuclear population with predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C216 document template sources and resolutions. Claims C217-C220 speculate that mature 60S model may be more accurate due to more structures available, potentially explaining observed differences. This is reasonable speculation but not directly tested. The discussion appropriately acknowledges model quality as potential confounding factor.

results.result: False positive rate is estimated at 0.6% for mature 60S-detected targets (28 expected in 4363), with even lower rate for targets detected by multiple templates; worst-case 6% for smallest EN 60S class is not expected to significantly affect classification.
results.evaluation: Claims C222-C224 describe threshold methodology allowing one false positive per image, likely an overestimate (Lucas et al., 2021). Claims C225-C226 calculate worst-case false positive rates and conclude minimal impact on classification. Claim C227 acknowledges need for adjusted thresholds for low-abundance targets. The false positive analysis is appropriately conservative.

results.result: Future improvements to 2DTM algorithm (correlation peak integration, peak profile fitting) could reduce overfitting and improve signal/noise separation, enabling classification of smaller/less abundant complexes and targets with smaller structural differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C228-C229, C234 propose future algorithmic improvements with citation to McDonough and Whalen, 1995. These are reasonable suggestions for future work but represent speculation about potential improvements rather than demonstrated capabilities. The suggestions are appropriate for discussion but do not constitute results of the current study.

results.result: Multiple factors (sample thickness, radiation damage, beam-induced motion, charging, frame alignment errors) cause high-resolution signal loss, making SNR ratios less sensitive to structural differences and biasing log2 values toward 0; systematic local noise differences may require context-specific biological controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C230-C231 list known factors affecting cryo-EM data quality and their expected effects on SNR ratios. Claims C232-C233 note cellular heterogeneity may affect classification and require biological controls. These are reasonable assessments of limitations based on established knowledge, appropriately discussed as factors requiring further research (C234).

results.result: Only three 60S templates were used; imperfect Gaussian fits and small cytoplasmic population with higher LN SNR suggest additional intermediates exist, requiring further investigation and additional templates to fully characterize spatiotemporal organization.
results.evaluation: Claim C235 states study scope. Claims C236-C237 note imperfect fits suggesting additional populations. Claims C239-C241 identify small cytoplasmic population with unexpected LN 60S preference, acknowledging uncertainty about interpretation. Claim C242 appropriately suggests future work. This represents honest assessment of study limitations and need for follow-up.

results.result: Multiple similar aligned templates require only single exhaustive search, with additional templates evaluated at detected locations/orientations, avoiding time-consuming searches; approach could be extended to library of alternate structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C197 describe methodological efficiency demonstrated in Figure 5, where template truncation analysis evaluates multiple templates at previously detected locations. Claim C198 suggests future extension to structure libraries. This represents an important practical advantage of the method, though library approach is speculative.

results.result: The approach could streamline model validation from in vitro/in silico experiments using few images; hypothetically, with complete conformational/compositional models, likelihood of specific structures could be calculated for individual molecules.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C202 propose potential applications for model validation and structure determination. These are speculative suggestions about future capabilities rather than demonstrated results. While conceptually reasonable extensions of the method, they represent hypothetical applications requiring substantial additional development.

results.result: Future studies establishing flux through assembly pathway are needed to test temporal lag hypothesis; 2DTM could study assembly kinetics by freezing cells at different time points after inhibiting specific maturation steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C248-C249 propose future experiments to test the temporal lag hypothesis (C247) and study assembly kinetics. These represent appropriate suggestions for follow-up work but are speculative proposals rather than results of the current study. The suggestions are reasonable but do not constitute demonstrated capabilities.
